transcript: I don't think I have ever been as fascinated by a film as I was with you can see everything, The new Nathan Fielder Elizabeth Holmes documentary. And what I really love about this film is that it really leans into just how unreliable every single narrator is in this film, including Nathan Fielder himself. And like, if you have seen any other Nathan Fielder project, it should not come as a surprise that Nathan Fielder has inserted himself as a character. But in the world of documentary filmmaking, it is pretty rare for the filmmaker to appear as a character in the film. Generally, they try to remain behind the scenes in an attempt to remain as unbiased as possible. Possible. But the problem is, no one is unbiased, especially when an edit is involved. Unconsciously or not, they are going to be shaping the story the way that they see it. And I love that this film really leans into that with Nathan. And acknowledges, yes, he does have his own biases, and it could be shaping what you are seeing right now. In fact, he is even directly called out on this at one point in the film by a person who was left out of the marketing. So I won't spoil who they are, but it's definitely something that the film is encouraging you to think about. In fact, there are so many little inconsistencies throughout that directly contradict something a person has said in the Film, whether that's Nathan himself, Liz, or her fiance Billy, who, Oh man, let me tell you, does not come across looking great in this film. But I really don't think that the film tells you how to feel about any of these people. And does a really good job capturing the complexity of these relationships. And especially when it comes to Elizabeth Holmes herself, The film very much asks the question: was she a victim or was she complicit? But it never comes to a firm conclusion. And I think it's gonna lead to some really fascinating conversations. And it's going to be a film that I am thinking about for a long time. Like, give it Best Picture. I'm not even joking.
